mentl/c5337a2:
The fanout's Threaded schedule now runs branches on host threads. The
spawn crossing had no unit of state: spawn banked the host thread id
while join dereferenced it as a record, the thread entry wrote its
completion and result words past the closure's allocation, the start
argument was a sentinel zero, and a spawned instance read a fresh
zeroed image. The task record answers all four at once — [task closure]
[completion][result], allocated per spawn through the one allocator,
banked whole in ThreadHandle, joined by an atomic wait on the
completion word.

Memory ownership follows the module's own proof (spawn_task in the
emit's fifth projection): a spawning module imports the shared image
per the wasi-threads convention, re-exports it for the p1 ABI, and
allocates through a compare-exchange cell at address 64, since
per-instance globals cannot serve two instances of one image; a
thread-free module keeps its defined memory, plain bump, and ships no
thread-spawn import at all. heap_mark/heap_reset go strategy-invariant
at the call site; the thread entry stamps per-instance identity into
tid_g and runs the top-level let inits the spawned instance needs.

threading.mn rewrote whole, 355 to 160 lines: the ffi/sentinel/
intrinsic block, the write-only threads ledger, num_cores (preview1
exposes no processor count), and the bypassed wasi_threads handler are
deleted; the wheel's dispatch chain drops its dead schedule installs
(a schedule installs lexically at the fanout it schedules). Two latent
surface bugs die with the audit: WaitResult's declaration order now
matches the wait32 ABI, and atomic_rmw gains a real tag dispatch with
two-operand cmpxchg as its own op.

mentl/c517b6f:
The synthetic demo builds its PAC signal inline; this reads a 4096-sample
recording from disk and runs the same comodulogram over it. A different
value origin — the path crosses WASI (fs_read_file_impl), splits on
newlines into view strings, and parses 4096 decimal lines into a native
[Float] list — so it stresses parse_float and the [Float] round-trip end
to end, where the inline demo only exercises literal-built floats.

tests/frontier/cfc-rec/oracle.py is a faithful numpy port of cfc.mn (the
same Hann single-bin DFT and raw Canolty MVL). The gate runs it over the
SAME on-disk bytes and asserts numpy's independent argmax agrees with
Mentl's. This is the representation-stress oracle the m3==m4 fixpoint is
structurally blind to: a byte-identical wheel can still corrupt user
float data, and only an independent implementation over the same data
catches it — a corrupt [Float] makes Mentl's argmax diverge from numpy's.

The recording carries a 6 Hz to 60 Hz coupling — the same well-resolved
low as the inline demo but a different high, so the file-transport
pipeline is proven to generalize, not memorize. Both implementations
argmax flat 7 (low index 1, high index 3). Seen RED first: a 6 to 40
recording shifts numpy and Mentl together to flat 5, so the expected-7
assertion is data-driven, never a constant the gate always sees.

Adds the cfc-rec link mode (CFC libs, run preopens /tmp) and run_cfc_rec
(copy the fixture to /tmp, assert Mentl's exit 42, then the numpy
cross-check when numpy is present, skipped-noted otherwise). Frontier
135 pass / 0 red; census 0; m2 == m3.

Also corrects three stale comments in cfc.mn left by the native-[Float]
migration: the phase/amp columns and the comodulogram matrix are
[Float], not scaled Int, and read_recording parses to [Float].

bits/c5ad571:
A pass used to be invisible. You could hear it and see it move, but you
could not find it, silence it, shorten it, or take one of five away
(audit F22, F23). Each one is now a span over the same time axis as the
timeline, in a panel that scrolls inside itself and keeps the playhead
running through it, so it can stay open while the bit plays.

A span belonging to a mouthed puppet is striped, because that is exactly
when it talks. The talker rule was the least visible thing in the engine
and is now the most visible thing in the panel.

What a span can do: mute (one MUTE, reversible from the same button),
shorten by dragging either edge or by fitting it to the stretch (one
TRIM), and come out entirely (one REMOVE, undoable for five seconds).
The engine already had all three; nothing could reach them.

Hearing one puppet on its own writes nothing. Solo builds the sim from a
project with the other passes stripped, exactly as blind recording does,
so listening never costs an undo. Both now go through one helper that
decides what the sim may see.

A stretch dragged on the axis is both the loop and the punch-in. Playing
goes round it; recording begins and ends inside it. A lap ends by
closing the open grabs and building a new sim from the project that now
contains them, because the sim only ever runs forward — which is what
makes the next lap play the pass you just performed. Punch-out is exact:
a pass stops where the stretch does, not two frames past it where
nothing would ever play it back.

Two fixes the lanes turned up. The halo's six 44px buttons are 264px
against a stage about 290 wide, so they fit only with nothing between
them; on a narrower phone, or the shorter stage the lanes leave, the bar
wraps to a second row rather than running off the edge with flip and
more unreachable. And a toast is news, not a wall: its body no longer
takes pointer events, and on the stage the stack clears the transport,
so an unrelated message can never block scrubbing.

stoop/c5ca0ac:
Three people were put in front of this cold and measured rather than
imagined: someone on a phone who scanned a code in a coffee shop,
someone emailed an issue file, and someone who wants paper. Two of the
three hit the same wall, and it was not the one that had been guessed at.

A page is 2.75 inches wide, which at 96dpi is 264 pixels, and the press
only ever scaled down to fit. So a page sat in 18 percent of a laptop
window with 11.5px body type, and on a phone it was 188 by 290 with
8.2px type — a postage stamp of the thing being made, with most of the
screen given over to background. The run now scales up to fill the
column, bounded by the window height so a page never grows taller than
the screen reading it, and a phone stacks the two pages of a spread
rather than cramming both across. The same phone now shows a page at 375
by 580 with 16.3px type, across 95 percent of the screen. A meter that
said "Everything fits on the paper" whenever nothing was wrong is
silent now, and the row above the page scrolls instead of wrapping, so
the page starts 134px down rather than 208.

A cutting's size is CSS pixels on the screen and was used as points on
paper: four pixels are three points, so every cutting was drawn a third
too large and a headline that sat on three lines wanted four. It is
converted now. But the deeper problem cannot be fixed by arithmetic: the
paper cannot know which faces the machine has — Impact on one, a
fallback on the next — so it should not be guessing. Each text cutting
records the lines its own browser broke it into, and the PDF draws those
lines. The screen is the layout; the paper obeys it.

The suite holds all of it: a page is readable on a phone and fills the
column on a laptop, and a headline breaks on paper where it broke on
screen with no word lost on the way. That last check first ran against a
page another test had already dropped text onto, and counted box height
instead of line boxes — it makes its own headline on its own page now,
and
